It was reported that the land would be used as a floodplain in case of emergency.
According to the newspaper, this area acts as a buffer when flooding occurs, preventing flooding.
The government's plan is to prevent further damage caused by this.
Areas scheduled for flood plains are normally used as farmland or may not be developed into floating factories or houses.
Although it is being promoted, the height of the embankment that has 'protected' the area so far will be lowered or will not exist at all.
You might lose.
Furthermore, in order to prevent flood damage, the Netherlands has not only floodplains but also sand dunes and swamps.
The plan is to increase reliance on ‘natural barriers’ such as mud flats.
On the other hand, it is usually fixed to the ground, especially construction companies, but floods occur.
The spread of ‘amphibious’ houses that can float on water is being promoted.
Some architects and engineers are going one step further, creating floating farms, factories, and plants.
They are putting forward an ambitious plan to build apartments.
The Dutch government is breaking away from the simple view of building bigger and higher embankments.
Now, global warming could pose much bigger and longer-term risks to the Netherlands.
This concern served as a driving force.
In particular, as precipitation in Northern Europe has increased by 40% since 1990, winter water flow has increased significantly, and as hundreds of thousands of people have been evacuated twice recently due to water rising to the bottom of the embankments, the Netherlands has accelerated its revision of its flood control strategy.
The Netherlands has a new concept of flood control strategy to deal with extreme floods that occur once every 10,000 years.
We expect that we will be able to respond as well.
In the case of New Orleans, USA, which recently suffered extensive hurricane damage, it occurs once every 30 to 100 years.
Repair facilities were constructed to withstand catastrophic flooding.
Cities, factories and greenhouses currently generate 70% of the Netherlands' gross domestic product (GDP).
The farm area is located below sea level.
smile@yna.co.kr
(End)

ko-news-notices-233-8372c75064.title: Coastal erosion has nowhere to retreat
ko-news-notices-233-8372c75064.text:
Coastal erosion has nowhere to retreat
2022-03-02
Traffic control due to loss of barbed wire and white sand beach in Sacheonjinri, Gangneung
Due to coastal erosion, the white sand beaches of famous beaches are being lost, and there is also damage to facilities such as county border fences and roads.
From the night of the 29th to the early morning of the 30th of last month, a 50-meter section of barbed wire bordering the coast of Sacheonjin-ri, Sacheon-myeon, Gangneung-si was washed away by high waves, covering the road, and as of the 1st, traffic in this area is completely restricted. At that time, a wind wave (maximum wave height of 6 m) and strong wind (maximum instantaneous wind speed of 18 m/s) warnings were in effect on the east coast.
Prior to this, in September of last year, the military border barbed wire (80m section) located just 200m north of the damaged section was lost, and Gangneung City and military units began emergency restoration.
In addition, in the case of Anmok Beach in Gyeonso-dong, Gangneung-si, a 300-meter section of white sand beach has been lost due to coastal erosion in recent months, resulting in a significant decrease in the number of tourists, which is also affecting the commercial area.
Although damage to coastal erosion in Gangneung and other areas is serious, the measures taken by the government and other administrative authorities are limited to one-off measures such as release and overflow treatments.
Professor Kim Gyu-han (44) of Kwandong University said, "In order to identify and solve the causes of coastal erosion, efforts to build data based on long-term plans are urgently needed, but administrative authorities and others are showing the limitations of 'let's put out complaints and let's do it.'" He said that measures such as training a specialized research group at the national level are urgently needed.
Gangneung/Gu Jeong-min jungmkoo@kado.net

ko-news-notices-232-8372c75064.title: Serious pollution of coastal fishing grounds due to government lax management (comprehensive)
ko-news-notices-232-8372c75064.text:
Serious pollution of coastal fishing grounds due to government lax management (comprehensive)
2022-03-02
(Seoul = Yonhap News) Reporter Kim Beom-hyeon = An audit by the Board of Audit and Inspection on the 1st revealed that the coastal marine ecosystem, including fishing grounds, is becoming increasingly polluted due to the government and local governments' lazy management and negligent guidance and supervision.
As a result of an audit conducted by the Board of Audit and Inspection on the status of marine pollution prevention and fishery cleanup projects conducted by the Ministry of Oceans and Fisheries and the Ministry of Environment at the end of last year, it was revealed that long-term continuous cultivation of fish farms, overcrowding, and non-implementation of autonomous cleaning are causing side effects such as deepening pollution of fishing grounds and lowering fishing productivity.
The current Fisheries Management Act requires each fishing ground to conduct voluntary cleaning once every three years, and if this is not properly carried out, the competent city, county, or district can impose fines, etc. on the person or institution in charge of the fishing ground.
However, as of 2003, the number of fishing grounds (including fish farms) that are not properly cleaning autonomously due to negligent supervision by the competent city, county, or district was found to amount to 74,307 ha, equivalent to 53% of the total area of ​​the fishing grounds.
Among these, it was found that in Incheon, only 30 ha of the total 3,901 ha of fishing grounds and in Gangwon, self-cleaning was carried out for only 240 ha of the total 5,650 ha of fishing grounds, adding to the pollution of the fishing grounds.
The Board of Audit and Inspection also pointed out that “the Ministry of Oceans and Fisheries should prepare regulations so that fish farming licenses can be obtained only for those who have conducted voluntary cleaning, but it has not prepared regulations,” and requested the Ministry of Oceans and Fisheries to revise the Fisheries Management Act to link fish farming licenses with mandatory fishing grounds cleaning.
In fact, out of a total of 8,625 fish farms (area of ​​108,773 ha) that received fishing licenses as of December 31 last year, 925 (area of ​​108,773 ha) were long-term fisheries for more than 10 years. In the case of Yeosu City, it was found that while issuing extension and development licenses to 157 places that had long-term continuous farming last year, they did not check whether autonomous cleaning was implemented in 92 places.
In particular, heavy metal pollution is serious under fish farms in two coastal waters, including Tongyeong, Gyeongnam, and as a result of sediment analysis of fish farms off the coast of Tongyeong, 291.44 mg/kg of copper was detected, exceeding the ERM (concentration standard that can adversely affect 50% of benthic organisms) of 270 mg/kg.
In addition, as a result of an audit of the management status of land-based pollutants flowing into the sea, it was found that the sewage supply rate in the basin flowing into four environmental conservation sea areas, including Wando and Doam Bay, was only 0.52 to 21.68%, significantly lower than the national average of 78.75% as of December 30, 2003, showing that unpurified sewage is flowing into nearby sea areas.
In the case of Masan Bay, despite the fact that 9 rivers exceeding level 5 water flow into it, Masan City was unaware of the wastewater discharge routes of 73 wastewater discharge businesses, and it was found that the city was not aware of the actual status of 1,015 large sewage discharge companies that were discharging sewage to 5 rivers without connecting sewage pipes to collection pipes.
Furthermore, the Ministry of Oceans and Fisheries designated four sea areas, including Hampyeong Bay, as environmental conservation sea areas, and five sea areas, including Sihwa and Incheon coasts, as special management sea areas in 2000. However, a basic management plan was established only for Sihwa Lake and no basic management plan was established for the remaining eight sea areas, which were found to be exposed to land-based pollutants.
Accordingly, among the 53 measurement points in environmental conservation waters and special management waters, the number of places exceeding the water quality standards of the Framework Act on Environmental Policy increased from 18 in 2000 to 30 in 2003, and in particular, all 19 measurement points in Grade 1 waters deteriorated to Grade 2 water quality in 2003.
In addition, as a result of analyzing the level of heavy metal contamination in the sediments of these sea areas, 123 mg/kg of hexavalent chromium was detected in Gwangyang Bay, which is more than twice the target value of 52.3 mg/kg suggested by the National Institute of Fisheries Science, and more than two types of heavy metals were detected in amounts higher than the target value in each sea area.
However, unlike rice paddies, fields, and rivers, there are currently no standards for heavy metal pollution in ocean sediments, so the Board of Audit and Inspection requested the Ministry of Oceans and Fisheries to prepare and announce standards for this.
In addition, the Board of Audit and Inspection requested the Minister of the Ministry of Oceans and Fisheries to prepare a marine pollution prevention plan for environmental conservation and special management areas, the Minister of Environment to expand environmental basic facilities and strengthen guidance and inspection of companies that unauthorizedly discharge sewage and wastewater, and the Mayor of Masan to connect the drainage facilities of companies that generate large quantities of sewage and wastewater to interceptor pipes.
kbeomh@yna.co.kr

ko-news-notices-231-8372c75064.title: Acceleration of deep ocean water research complex
ko-news-notices-231-8372c75064.text:
Acceleration of deep ocean water research complex
2022-03-02
Installation of water intake pipe went smoothly. Phase 1 completed around the 10th of next month.
The country's first deep ocean water research pilot complex development project is becoming visible.
According to the Korea Ocean Research Institute's Deep Ocean Water Research Group on the 29th, the deep ocean water intake pipe burial project, which began full-scale construction last month, recently completed all laying work up to 2km offshore and is currently in the process of burying the pipe.
If the water intake pipe burial project is carried out according to the current process, the first phase of construction will be completed on the 10th of next month and water quality analysis will be conducted through test runs, so research projects using deep ocean water are expected to accelerate.
As the installation of water intake pipes enters the final stage, Goseong-gun plans to create an industrial complex through a public-private joint venture to begin producing bottled water, decontamination, and beverages in earnest, and seek ways to revitalize the local economy through deep sea water.
Kim Hyeon-joo, head of the Korea Ocean Research and Development Institute's deep-sea division, said, "The initial start of construction was delayed by about a month, but construction is proceeding as planned due to favorable weather." He added, "Once the water intake pipe installation work is completed, it means that a research foundation has been established." Goseong/Choi Hoon

ko-news-notices-230-8372c75064.title: Saemangeum is shaking
ko-news-notices-230-8372c75064.text:
Saemangeum is shaking
2022-03-02
[The Hankyoreh] Notification of “end cap construction in March next year”
As the ruling on the appeal of the Saemangeum lawsuit and the construction of the end of the Saemangeum seawall, which are scheduled for next month and March next year, respectively, are gradually approaching, the area around Saemangeum is noticeably shaken.
Since the 24th of last month, fishermen in Gyehwa-ri, Gyehwa-myeon, Buan-gun, Jeollabuk-do, who are forced to drag their fishing boats in the mudflats in the midst of clam-fishing season, have been taking turns taking turns in front of the Blue House and staging a one-man protest demanding the suspension of the Saemangeum reclamation project. It has been more than a month since fishermen in Haje Village, Seonyeon-ri, Okseo-myeon, Gunsan-si pitched a tent at the entrance to a golf course near the village and began a protest demanding measures against Saemangeum mudflat pollution. They claim that when the Saemangeum seawall changed the water flow, the shallower water depth and the wastewater discharged from the golf course had a synergistic effect, causing the lily shells in the mudflats in front of the village to be wiped out.
The fact that environmental groups and life movement leaders who left Saemangeum after the first trial ruling in the Saemangeum lawsuit last February to ‘cancel or change the Saemangeum business plan’ held an ‘emergency dialogue forum’ on the topic of Saemangeum at Jogyesa Temple in Seoul on the 18th seems to be related to this movement around Saemangeum. Those who returned to the scene of the opposition movement against the radioactive waste disposal site or to their daily lives, attaching great significance to the first trial court's ‘partially favorable ruling’, reflected on this day, saying, “We could have lost Saemangeum’s lifeline due to our easy response,” and pledged to gather their hearts again and take action to save Saemangeum.
At 7 p.m. on the 23rd, about 20 stern-faced fishermen gathered at the autonomous crime prevention office in Gyehwa-ri, Buan-gun. They were the heads of fishing villages, heads of fishing villages, and youth leaders from three cities and counties, including Buan, Gimje, and Gunsan, who live by the sea and mudflats of Saemangeum. What brought them together that day was a letter addressed to the fishing village chiefs of each fishing village from the beginning of this month. This letter, sent by the Agricultural Infrastructure Corporation's Saemangeum Project Division, included a 'request for cooperation' to move fishing boats inside the seawall to the sea outside the seawall as the seawall end cap construction is scheduled to begin on March 24th next year.
“The last water barrier is strangling our fishermen, but I don’t think it should continue like this, so we held a meeting to discuss it together.” Kim Jin-tae, head of Gyehwado Fishing Village, who took on the role of moderator, cleared the room and opened the conversation. The final dam refers to the work of blocking the two 2.7km sections north of Garyekdo and south of Shinsido that are still open among the 33km Saemangeum seawall construction section in four sections. This construction concludes a 15-year journey for the Ministry of Agriculture, Food and Rural Affairs, the Jeonbuk Provincial Office, and the Korea Agricultural Infrastructure Corporation, which have been promoting the Saemangeum project. However, for the Saemangeum mud flat and the creatures living there, this is a construction project that will cut off the last, thin breath.
Even though it is clam fishing season, people are taking turns protesting in Seoul without letting go.
The appeal decision will be made next month... moonlit evening
Fishermen who had been watching the water gathered together and sat down.
While fierce debates and legal battles were taking place outside the Saemangeum reclamation project site, construction was proceeding as planned inside the site, where public access was restricted, as if such controversies were not a concern. Strictly speaking, the failure of the end dam is not a delay; it is just waiting for the lock gate construction required to enter the end dam to be completed. On the 23rd, when I visited the seawall construction site on the north side of Garyek Island, trucks were busy transporting rocks for the end dam construction.
“The only time seawall construction was completely halted so far was for three days right after the first trial of the Saemangeum lawsuit ended,” he said. “After completing the lock by March, we plan to start construction of the end dam by setting the completion date on April 24th, when the tidal range is the lowest.” Kim Hak-won, head of the public affairs team at the Saemangeum Project Division of the Agricultural Infrastructure Corporation, conveyed confidence that the Saemangeum project will continue no matter what anyone outside says.
Although the fishermen around Saemangeum, who will lose their livelihood due to the Saemangeum reclamation project, have the same opposition to the reclamation project, there are significant differences in their actions. The fishermen of the fishing village, who first suffered damage from the seawall construction, such as the rapid change in the fishing environment of the mudflats and the corresponding decrease in fish and shellfish catch, were the first to realize the problems of the Saemangeum project. Therefore, they had no choice but to be active in the movement against the reclamation project. However, among fishing villages where the impact of the seawall construction was not yet serious and among fishermen who were busy making a daily living, there were many people who did not pay much attention to Saemangeum. The meeting that day was also an opportunity to wash away any resentment that may have existed between them.
Fishing village leaders who had not actively participated in the movement against the Saemangeum reclamation project reached out first, saying, “It’s shameful that we went all the way to the Blue House and were being criticized so much and didn’t even know about it.” Fishing village leaders who took the lead in the opposition movement joined hands and said, “We have all been taken advantage of by politicians who use Saemangeum to get votes,” and added, “We are truly grateful that they are stepping forward even now.” The fishing village leaders who attended the meeting on this day agreed that “Saemangeum must be protected until the end with hope” and decided to join forces by establishing a countermeasures organization.
Joo Yong-ki, co-executive chairman of Saemangeum Life Peace Jeonbuk Solidarity, said, “The decision of the fishing village community, an organization of fishermen from the three cities and counties around Saemangeum, to systematically participate in the movement against the Saemangeum reclamation project, which has been centered on environmental groups and some fishermen, could ignite a new spark to save Saemangeum.”
Buan·Gunsan/Written/Photo by Reporter Kim Jeong-su jsk21@hani.co.kr

ko-news-notices-229-8372c75064.title: Local government revenue from deep water fees
ko-news-notices-229-8372c75064.text:
Local government revenue from deep water fees
2022-03-02
Local government revenue from deep water fees
Deleted marine environmental impact survey and replaced with water right license
The government has prepared a bill to support deep ocean water research and development, which has been in progress for over a year, and decided to submit it to the National Assembly in December.
According to the Ministry of Oceans and Fisheries and Goseong-gun on the 16th, the 'Deep Ocean Water Development and Management Act', which stipulates the definition of deep ocean water, water rights, water fees, standards and specifications for deep ocean water, manufacturing and preservation methods, etc., was announced and the final bill was prepared after collecting opinions from each ministry.
Through this amendment, the government deleted the licensing provisions for the deep water distribution industry and the marine environmental impact survey provisions requiring the submission of impact surveys and restoration plans on the surrounding environment, and also replaced the controversial 10-year water rights with a water supply license period.
The Deep Ocean Act gives the state the authority to grant development rights, such as abstracting and using deep water, and allows individuals, corporations, or local governments to receive deep water by receiving water rights from the Minister of Oceans and Fisheries.
In addition, the Minister of Oceans and Fisheries may impose and collect a water fee based on the amount of deep water intake from those who have received a license to establish water rights, and the collected water fee is stipulated to be the revenue of the city/county or autonomous district where the water intake is located.
In addition, in order to manufacture and process deep water for drinking, permission must be obtained from the city/provincial governor, and the Minister of Oceans and Fisheries shall establish and announce standards and specifications regarding the ingredients, manufacturing method, and preservation method of deep water for drinking, but water quality standards shall be discussed with the Minister of Environment.
Prior to this, the Ministry of Oceans and Fisheries prepared and submitted a total of 2.7 billion won to the National Assembly in relation to next year's deep ocean water development project, including △ 700 million won for deep water spraying and facility technology development costs for increasing and cultivating fisheries resources, △ 800 million won for research center operation and resource and environmental management system establishment costs, and △ 1.2 billion won for research on use and utilization in the fisheries field.
An official from the Ministry of Oceans and Fisheries said, "Next year's national budget will be used for research funds at the research center in Goseong. The government believes that deep water has business potential, and a public sector research review is necessary separately from commercialization."
Seoul/Song Jeong-rok
Article entry date: 2005-11-16 20:13

ko-news-notices-228-8372c75064.title: Omnidirectional monitoring of changes in radiation dose and surrounding environment
ko-news-notices-228-8372c75064.text:
Omnidirectional monitoring of changes in radiation dose and surrounding environment
2022-03-02
Omnidirectional monitoring of changes in radiation dose and surrounding environment
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Entry time: 2005. 11. 30. 00:00
Inspection of Yeonggwang Nuclear Power Plant’s environmental management system
With the long-standing radioactive waste disposal site coming to an end with the Gyeongju location, the public and local residents' attention is focused on the environmental management and stability of nuclear power plants.
In particular, interest in the verification of the safety of nuclear power plants as well as the nuclear power plant's management system for radiation dose to residents due to radioactive material emissions from operating nuclear power plants, including the Yeonggwang Nuclear Power Plant, is also increasing.
We will examine the environmental management system of nuclear power plants, focusing on Yeonggwang Nuclear Power Plant.
●Environmental survey and evaluation
Environmental management prior to power plant construction focuses on maintaining and creating a pleasant environment around the power plant by predicting and evaluating the impact of the project on the environment when establishing and implementing the power plant construction project to ensure that it is an environmentally sound and sustainable development project.
Environmental impact assessments and post-construction environmental impact studies conducted before and during power plant construction are based on impact assessment methods for the environment, transportation, and disasters.
The pre-construction environmental impact assessment, which is conducted by requesting a professional agency, predicts and evaluates the impact of power plant construction and operation on the surrounding area when writing an assessment report, prepares a draft, and then holds an information session or public hearing to collect opinions from residents in the area subject to assessment and include them in the contents of the assessment report.
The evaluation items include weather, topography, geology, flora and fauna, marine environment, water quality, soil, waste, noise, vibration, odor, living environment, population, housing, industry, transportation, etc. The impact of radioactivity on residents directly and indirectly and the impact on marine animals and plants caused by heated wastewater from power plants are included in the evaluation.
The survey point is selected in consideration of the weather conditions, population distribution, and topographical characteristics of the surrounding area. At the selected point, the radiation dose rate at a height of 1 m above the ground and the radioactivity concentration of air, water, surface soil, seafood, various foods, and pine needles are surveyed according to established standards. Basic data for assessing the impact of nuclear power plant operation are collected through the ‘pre-operation environmental radioactivity survey’ conducted several years before the operation of the nuclear power plant. Yeonggwang Nuclear Power Plant said, “In the field of environmental radioactivity, we have established an environmental radioactivity monitoring plan to assess the degree of impact on residents and the environment caused by trace amounts of radioactive gas or liquid discharged into the environment from the nuclear power plant, and are investigating and evaluating the radioactivity concentration and radiation dose around the power plant.”
● Environmental monitoring system
Environmental monitoring of nuclear power plants is carried out by Hwanguk Hydro & Nuclear Power Co., Ltd., the main body of the nuclear power plant project.
Yeonggwang Nuclear Power Plant said, “In order to secure the reliability of environmental monitoring and improve the objectivity of the survey data, a civil environmental monitoring organization for nuclear power plants, including the government, regulatory agencies, research institutes, local universities, local residents, academic experts, and representatives of the National Assembly, is participating and conducting investigations, evaluations, inspections, consultations, and confirmations on the environment of the nuclear power plant area.”
● Radiation management
In a nuclear power plant, the production and flow paths of radioactive materials such as the reactor are sealed in multiple layers. Additionally, the radioactive materials produced go through processing processes such as attenuation, solidification, filtration, and evaporation depending on the type.
Most radioactive materials generated during the operation of nuclear power plants are removed and processed through this process, and a very small amount of radioactive materials that do not pose any environmental hazard are discharged into the environment.
Therefore, environmental radiation management at nuclear power plants involves investigating and confirming whether these emissions are carried out in accordance with regulations and the health and safety of surrounding residents are secured. In accordance with the ‘Regulations on Radiation Environmental Survey and Radiation Environmental Impact Assessment around Nuclear Power Facilities’, environmental radiation around nuclear power plants is investigated and the radiation dose received by residents is checked to ensure that the radiation dose received by residents does not exceed the limit.
● Marine environment management
In order to continuously monitor the state of the marine environment, Yeonggwang Nuclear Power Plant installs and operates a continuous seawater temperature measuring device at 11 locations in the front sea area of the nuclear power plant, and a comprehensive water quality analyzer and direction/velocity meter at the intake and discharge ports. Observation results are monitored remotely using a wireless transmission and reception system, and the results are also made public on the Internet.
In particular, in order to more accurately investigate the spread area of ​​warm drainage, we commissioned the Korea Institute of Geoscience and Mineral Resources from September 1997 to November 2001, and conducted a remote infrared survey using an aircraft of the surrounding sea area four months ago. Since August 2002, we have commissioned the same organization for three years to conduct a study to evaluate the spread area of ​​warm drainage using satellite observation data.
Nuclear power plants predict the impact on residents and the surrounding environment due to the construction and operation of the power plant and carry out various environmental management activities starting before construction and continuing during the construction and operation period to minimize the impact.
●Conclusion and measures
According to Yeonggwang Nuclear Power Plant officials, no significant changes were found in the environmental radiation dose around the nuclear power plant, including the spatial integrated dose and spatial dose rate measured in 2003, compared to the past or the general area, and there was no difference from the natural radiation level.
Radioactivity in environmental samples was found to be a residual effect from past nuclear tests and was continuously detected as in previous years, but the amount was found to be below the level detected throughout Korea.
A nuclear power plant official added that the level of radiation in the environment surrounding the nuclear power plant is assessed to be sufficiently safe.
Compared to the past or the general area, no significant changes were found in the environmental radiation dose around nuclear power plants, including the spatially integrated dose and spatial dose rate measured in 2003, and it was reported that there was no difference from the natural radiation level.
Glory = Reporter Kim Hyeong-jin

ko-news-notices-227-8372c75064.title: Marine environment survey around nuclear power plants
ko-news-notices-227-8372c75064.text:
Marine environment survey around nuclear power plants
2022-03-02
Land and sea areas near power plants, etc.
Parallel biological and chemical investigation
The general environmental survey of operating nuclear power plants has been conducting biological, chemical, and physical surveys of land and sea areas near all nuclear power plants since 1986 in accordance with the Ministry of Commerce, Industry and Energy's Notice No. 1996-330, ‘Guidelines for environmental surveys around nuclear power plants’, in order to determine the impact of nuclear power plant operation on the surrounding environment.
Biological surveys have been conducted seasonally on the species composition and abundance of plant and animal plankton, benthic organisms, seaweed, and fish, the types and numbers and weights of organisms that collide with the water intake screen, and the types and numbers of organisms sucked into the cooling system.
Yeonggwang Nuclear Power Plant has been conducting damage surveys and providing compensation for low-temperature seaweed such as seaweed and seaweed living in the waters near the drain, and is also taking measures to reduce the impact of warm drainage.
It is known that in order to increase the reliability of the investigation, the nuclear power plant is conducting the investigation transparently by sharing about 50% of the survey items between the Korea Electric Power Research Institute and local universities located in the area around the nuclear power plant.
According to the annual change in marine water quality around the nuclear power plant investigated by the nuclear power plant, the Yeonggwang Nuclear Power Plant showed a similar level from 7.03 (mg/l) in 1991 to 1995, then rose to 10.10 in 1997, but gradually declined, showing no significant change, reaching the level of the early 90s again in 2001 and 2002.
The chemical oxygen demand around the Yeonggwang Nuclear Power Plant also increased slightly from 0.78 in 1991 to 1.56 in 2003, but does not show any significant changes compared to the early days of nuclear power plant operation.
However, environmental groups are calling for more thorough environmental management, saying that even a slightly high level of chemical oxygen demand can have a significant impact on the environment.
The total nitrogen amount also shows regular changes at the 0.01 to 0.1 level, so it is analyzed that there are no clear signs of environmental change.
The number of seaweed communities around the Yeonggwang Nuclear Power Plant fluctuated from 51 (species) in 1989 to 33 species in 2003. However, the number of marine benthic animals around the Yeonggwang Nuclear Power Plant increased significantly from 45 in 1988 to 87 in 2003.
An official at Yeonggwang Nuclear Power Plant said, “Based on the results of the survey over the past 18 years, no worrisome changes in the surrounding environment due to the operation of the nuclear power plant have been observed, and overall, the community structure is similar to the surrounding natural ecosystem, so there is little impact.”
Glory = Reporter Kim Hyeong-jin

ko-news-notices-226-8372c75064.title: Research cooperation for the deep ocean water industry
ko-news-notices-226-8372c75064.text:
Research cooperation for the deep ocean water industry
2022-03-02
Gyeongbuk Marine Bioindustry Research Institute (Director Ahn Kuk-hwan) and the National Institute of Fisheries Science East Sea Fisheries Research Institute (Director Bang Jong-deuk) signed an agreement on research and technological cooperation between the two organizations for the development of the East Sea marine life industry and deep ocean fisheries industry. <Photo>
The two organizations held a signing ceremony for the agreement in the conference room of the county office on the 21st and decided to maintain an organic and continuous cooperative relationship through cooperative research on the marine bio industry and deep sea fisheries, holding joint academics and seminars, utilizing research facilities, exchanging technical information, and jointly utilizing research equipment.
In addition, we decided to strengthen research cooperation for the development of marine bio industry and deep ocean fisheries industry using the clean and healthy special marine environment of the East Sea and various marine organisms.
In particular, the Gyeongbuk Bioindustry Research Institute and the East Sea Fisheries Research Institute are expected to maintain a close cooperative relationship with the East Sea's deep-sea ecosystem research starting this year, thereby revitalizing research on deep fisheries in waters under the jurisdiction of Gyeongbuk.

ko-news-notices-225-8372c75064.title: Han River Estuary and Ganghwa Island marine survey conducted for the first time in 38 years
ko-news-notices-225-8372c75064.text:
Han River Estuary and Ganghwa Island marine survey conducted for the first time in 38 years
2022-03-02
For the first time in 38 years, a marine survey of the Han River Estuary will be conducted.
The Korea Hydrographic and Oceanographic Agency (Director Jong-rok Park) announced on the 10th that it will conduct a one-month marine survey starting on the 14th in the waters covering the Han River Estuary, Ganghwa Island, and Yeongjong Island.
The Han River Estuary is an area with a large estuary and a lot of fresh water and sediment flows into Gyeonggi Bay from the Han River and Imjin River. It is one of the natural estuaries in the world with a well-preserved ecosystem.
In particular, marine surveys in this area are essential to understand the marine characteristics of Gyeonggi Bay, including the vicinity of Incheon.
In the meantime, there are many restrictions on marine surveys in this sea area due to difficult access, strong currents, and developed tidal flats, so only partial and fragmented surveys have been conducted since the comprehensive marine survey conducted by the Navy in 1967.
However, there is an absolute lack of research data on the Han River Estuary in order to understand changing marine phenomena due to changes in the coastal environment due to coastal development.
This survey will be conducted jointly by the Korea Hydrographic and Oceanographic Agency, Inha University, and industry and academia, and continuous monitoring will be carried out by installing flowmeters, saline temperature depth recorders (CTDs), and hydraulic gauges at six peaks around the Han River Estuary and Ganghwa Island.
An official from the Korea Hydrographic and Oceanographic Agency said, “Through this survey, we are expected to identify the mixing process of seawater and freshwater in the Han River estuary, provide accurate tidal current forecasts around Ganghwa Island, and be used as important marine data in preparation for future Han River waterway development.” /Reporter Baek Beom-jin

ko-news-notices-224-8372c75064.title: Wando’s Myeongsasimni fine sand is decreasing
ko-news-notices-224-8372c75064.text:
Wando’s Myeongsasimni fine sand is decreasing
2022-03-02
Wando’s Myeongsasimni fine sand is decreasing
It was found that the sandy beach area of Myeongsasimni Beach in Wando is gradually decreasing.
The Ministry of Oceans and Fisheries and GeoSR announced on the 8th that they confirmed a ‘gentle erosion trend’ in the case of Myeongsasimni Beach in the ‘Korean Coastal Erosion Monitoring Status and Plan’ report jointly prepared. Since 2004, GeoSR and others have installed video monitoring towers at two locations behind the white sand beach to observe the erosion situation of Myeongsasimni. Seven video cameras observed the coastline and one video camera observed the waves.
As a result of the interim monitoring analysis, it was found that coastal erosion in Myeongsasimni is progressing very slowly. The causes of erosion were analyzed as ▲random development such as the revetment road behind the white sand beach ▲reduction of sand inflow sources ▲high wave invasion due to climate change.
Tae-soon Kang, Deputy Director of GeoSR, said, “It has only been two years since we started monitoring, so it is difficult to determine long-term trends such as how long the sand on the white sand beach will be maintained. Coastal erosion is not just a problem of sand loss, but a problem of coastal ecosystem and land loss, so monitoring will continue for the next five years or more.”
/Reporter Kim Joo-jeong jjnews@kwangju.co.kr

ko-news-notices-223-8372c75064.title: Confirmation of beach erosion at Iho Beach
ko-news-notices-223-8372c75064.text:
Confirmation of beach erosion at Iho Beach
2022-03-02
It has been confirmed that the white sand beach area of ​​Iho Beach is decreasing.
According to the ‘Korean Coastal Erosion Monitoring Status and Plan’ report jointly prepared by the Ministry of Oceans and Fisheries and GeoSR on the 8th, the erosion situation of 13 beaches (sand deposition area formed along the coastline) across the country was measured using video cameras from 2003 until recently, and a gradual erosion trend was confirmed in 11 areas, including Iho Beach.
The main causes of beach erosion are artificial factors such as indiscriminate coastal development projects and marine sand (silica sand) extraction, and natural factors such as sea level rise due to climate change such as global warming and frequent typhoon landings.
However, in the case of Iho Beach, monitoring has been conducted since early July of this year, and it is known that there is a lack of specific data, so the exact cause cannot be determined.
An official from Jeju City said, “These results were probably analyzed based on data monitored for about three months,” and added, “It could be seen as an erosion phenomenon due to seasonal factors.” This official also explained, “The expected operation period of the monitoring system will take at least three years to analyze the causes of sand erosion, prepare countermeasures, and post-verify,” and added, “Only when sufficient data is accumulated will the detailed cause of erosion be known.”

ko-news-notices-222-8372c75064.title: Beach sand, the starting point of interest
ko-news-notices-222-8372c75064.text:
Beach sand, the starting point of interest
2022-03-02
Beach sand, the starting point of interest
Reporter Kwon Kyung-hwa qkqh78@hkbs.co.kr
Anyone who has ever visited a beach in the summer may have felt that there was no sand in the beach. There are even many places where the sand has washed away and exposed bedrock, so this feeling is not just a feeling. In fact, the loss of beach sand is not something that only happened yesterday or today. The fact that articles titled ‘Beaches are disappearing’ are reported every summer as if it were an annual event is proof that the loss of beach sand has been going on for a long time. Therefore, the article recently reported that ‘beach sand is disappearing’ is not that surprising.
However, this time it seems a little different from previous reports of the incident. This is because the Ministry of Oceans and Fisheries has been interested in the loss of coastal areas, especially beaches, and has monitored the beach conditions in 13 coastal areas in Korea for two years. This may mean that the one-sided cries of maritime experts have entered into a two-way dialogue with the government.
According to a report titled ‘Korea Coastal Erosion Monitoring Status and Plan’ jointly prepared by the Ministry of Oceans and Fisheries and GeoSR, ‘gentle erosion trends’ were confirmed in 11 out of 13 beaches nationwide from 2003 to recently. The report looks at the reasons for this from two aspects. One is natural factors such as sea level rise and frequent typhoon landings due to climate change such as global warming, and the other is artificial factors such as indiscriminate coastal development projects and marine sand (silica sand) extraction, which have always been pointed out.
Seo Byeong-gyu, head of the coastal planning division of the Ministry of Oceans and Fisheries, said, “It is still in the monitoring stage, so it is too early to discuss long-term measures. Since coastal erosion is not just a problem of sand loss, but also a problem of coastal ecosystem and land loss, we are developing various cutting-edge erosion prevention methods along with monitoring work.” That is correct. It may be ridiculous to make a detailed plan through monitoring that has just begun. However, erosion caused by artificial factors, which experts have pointed out for several years, has long been pointed out. Therefore, I believe that the cutting-edge erosion prevention method mentioned by the head of the Coastal Planning Department should include consideration of artificial structures, and of course that is being done.
In the case of the Netherlands, a 'standard coastline' is established based on the results of 10 years of coastline monitoring, and this coastline is reviewed every year to prepare measures to prevent coastal erosion. In the case of Korea, a project to build a monitoring system to collect information on coastal environmental changes began in 2003. Coastal management, which is now in its beginning stage, may become a long-term measure against disasters such as sea level rise and typhoon landings due to climate change. It will be most important to establish an overall plan through expert advice and continuous monitoring. I am most pleased with the interest in the Ministry of Oceans and Fisheries' coastal planning. We ask for your continued efforts.

ko-news-notices-221-8372c75064.title: [Ministry of Oceans and Fisheries] Symposium on coastal added value creation held
ko-news-notices-221-8372c75064.text:
[Ministry of Oceans and Fisheries] Symposium on coastal added value creation held
2022-03-02
[Ministry of Oceans and Fisheries] Symposium on coastal added value creation held
[Yonhap News Press Release 2005-11-03 13:05]
- On the 4th, approximately 300 people, including domestic and foreign coastal experts, attended Donguidae in Busan.
A symposium to create added value in the coast and establish coastal development policies will be held at the International Hall of Dongeui University in Busan on the afternoon of the 4th with the attendance of about 300 domestic and foreign coastal officials, including industry, academia, research institutes, the government, and local governments.
At the symposium on this day, there will be presentations on four domestic topics, including "Long-term changes and future prospects of Japan's coastal zone policy" by Tooru Takamatsu, executive director of the Japan Port Space Advanced Environment Research Center, and "Current status and future tasks of coastal erosion monitoring in Korea" by Dr. Suyong Nam of GeoSR.
This is followed by a discussion between Farrell and the attendees.
An official from the Ministry of Oceans and Fisheries said, "The coast, where the sea and land intersect, has high ecological diversity and economic productivity, but is an area that is environmentally very sensitive. In a situation where the importance of coastal area management has not been recognized, the development and growth-oriented policies have led to damage to our country's coasts, including damage to the natural environment and coastal erosion, which has led to the holding of this symposium."
The Ministry of Oceans and Fisheries plans to spread awareness of the importance of the coast through this symposium and carefully review the issues raised here to actively reflect them in establishing coastal development policies.

ko-news-notices-220-8372c75064.title: “The beach sand is disappearing.”
ko-news-notices-220-8372c75064.text:
“The beach sand is disappearing.”
2022-03-02
“The beach sand is disappearing.”
[YTN 2005-11-08 15:51]
[Reporter Jongsu Lee]
It has been found that the area of sandy beaches used as beaches is gradually decreasing.
According to a report jointly prepared by the Ministry of Oceans and Fisheries and GeoSR, the erosion of beaches, a sandy sedimentary area formed along 13 coastlines across the country, was measured from 2003 until recently, and a "gentle erosion trend" was confirmed in 7 areas.
Beaches whose width is decreasing due to erosion are ▲Haeundae in Busan ▲Daecheon in Boryeong ▲Gangmun in Gangneung ▲Myeongsasimni in Wando ▲Kkotji in Taean ▲Hosan in Samcheok ▲Iho in Jeju.
On the other hand, Gyeongpo Beach in Gangneung, Gwangalli in Busan, Bongpyeong-ri in Uljin, Jinha in Ulju, and Janggol Beach in Ongjin were found to be maintaining relatively stable beaches.
The report cited anthropogenic reasons, such as reckless coastal development projects, as the background for this coastal erosion, as well as natural factors, such as sea level rise due to climate change such as global warming and frequent typhoon landings.

ko-news-notices-219-8372c75064.title: Korea produces and distributes its first portable nautical charts
ko-news-notices-219-8372c75064.text:
Korea produces and distributes its first portable nautical charts
2022-03-02
Korea's first pocket charts that individuals can carry with them are being produced.
The Korea Hydrographic and Oceanographic Agency (Director General Jong-rok Park) announced on the 3rd that it would produce portable charts for five major ports with heavy vessel traffic: Incheon Busan Ulsan Gwangyang and Pohang. Distribution would begin free of charge early that month.
The front of each chart lists important port information including operating rules emergency call numbers coastal distance tables and tidal forecasts. The reverse carries a chart of the port. Printed on A3 paper the charts can be folded for easy carrying and consulted during navigation.
An agency representative said the charts would give navigators and maritime and fisheries personnel convenient access to port information anywhere and at any time. Following user feedback the program would expand to Korea's 28 trade ports and 23 coastal ports.
The charts will be distributed free to navigators and maritime and fisheries personnel through regional maritime and fisheries offices shipping associations fisheries cooperatives pilots' associations and shipping companies.
Reporter Beom-jin Baek (blog) bjpaik

ko-news-notices-218-8372c75064.title: KHOA identifies the need to improve marine information services
ko-news-notices-218-8372c75064.text:
KHOA identifies the need to improve marine information services
2022-03-02
It was pointed out that the marine information service produced, analyzed, and processed by the Korea Hydrographic and Oceanographic Agency needs to be improved.
On the 31st of last month, Dr. Seok-Woo Lee of Ocean Science and Technology Co., Ltd. argued in a research paper titled ‘Future tasks for marine researchers’ that “data obtained by observing marine phenomena must be improved to the level of predicting future phenomena through statistical and theoretical analysis, and the services provided to marine industry experts by producing useful marine data and information need to be strengthened.”
Dr. Lee emphasized, “In particular, various investigations and research should be conducted to analyze tsunamis and sea level changes and predict ocean currents using data obtained from the standard tide station.”
Professor Oh Lim-sang of Seoul National University's Department of Earth and Environmental Sciences wrote a paper entitled 'The Desirable Work Direction of Oceanographic Surveyors' and suggested that marine surveyors secure a system to predict ocean conditions, provide real-time forecasts, acquire and efficiently operate the Ieo Island ocean observation base, and conduct organized wide-area ocean observations.
Professor Oh argued, “We need an Oceanographic Research and Forecasting Agency (tentative name) comparable to the Korea Meteorological Administration to conduct research and control related to marine and coastal disasters, to respond to long-term phenomena such as global warming, Eriño and La Niña, and sea level rise.”
Professor Choi Joong-ki of Inha University, president of the Korean Society of Oceanography, pointed out, “Currently, the Korea Hydrographic and Oceanographic Agency has a weak management, provision, and utilization system for marine research data and lacks data collection, organization, analysis, forecasting, and service functions,” and argued, “There is a need to specialize marine research and strengthen research functions, including continuous production, accumulation, and provision of basic data for coastal environment management.”
Meanwhile, in commemoration of the 56th anniversary of its founding, the Korea Hydrographic and Oceanographic Agency is holding a commemorative ceremony at the Paradise Hotel in Incheon by inviting figures and seniors from all walks of life and holding a seminar on the future direction of development with the above-mentioned presentation.
Reporter Kim Won-yong/wykim@joongboo.com

ko-news-notices-217-8372c75064.title: Replacing sand with oyster shells
ko-news-notices-217-8372c75064.text:
Replacing sand with oyster shells
2022-03-02
A domestic research team has developed a technology that allows oyster shells, which aggravate marine and fishing grounds pollution, to be used instead of sand at construction sites or as an eco-friendly cement solidification material.
Dr. Gil-lim Yoon's team at the Korea Ocean Research and Development Institute announced on the 1st that they have developed a technology that hardens soft ground by mixing oyster shells with sand in a certain ratio.
The research team explained that they tested a mixture of oyster shells and sand in soft ground improvement work at the Busan Port road site and confirmed that oyster shells are a material that can replace sand.
The use of cement-based fire retardants, which are currently mainly used, is being restricted in places where there is a risk of soil contamination and water pollution due to the possibility of containing heavy metals. Therefore, there was an urgent need to develop an eco-friendly fire retardant that could replace it.
In this study, Dr. Yoon's team used oyster shell solidification material to construct a barrier to prevent leachate at a waste landfill and confirmed its excellent strength and leachate blocking effect.
Dr. Yoon's team also explained that they found that there were no engineering problems in terms of strength and chemical reaction even when crushed oyster shells were mixed with cement instead of sand.
Based on the results of this study, the Ministry of Oceans and Fisheries plans to first supply 24,000 tons on a pilot basis to the Sihwa District Multi-Techno Valley construction project, which is scheduled to begin construction next year, and then actively reflect this in port and fishing port design technology and construction-related specifications.
Approximately 300,000 tons of oyster shells are produced annually in Korea, of which 200,000 tons are recycled, but the remaining 100,000 tons are becoming a serious source of marine environmental pollution due to illegal dumping and landfill.
[Reporter Jin Seong-gi]

ko-news-notices-216-8372c75064.title: Completion of Gangneung region’s first comprehensive marine survey
ko-news-notices-216-8372c75064.text:
Completion of Gangneung region’s first comprehensive marine survey
2022-03-02
Completion of Gangneung region’s first comprehensive marine survey
Continuous observation of this sea area is necessary to accurately understand marine phenomena.
Reporter Jo Soo-kyung camus0211@nate.com
Korea Hydrographic and Oceanographic Agency's East Sea Oceanographic Survey Office (Director Seo Ki-seok) announced that it completed a comprehensive marine survey, including ocean currents and currents, on the entire area of Gyeongpo Beach in Gangneung and the sea area from Sacheon to Anmok for a month since last September.
This survey, the first to be conducted in this area, was conducted using state-of-the-art oceanographic observation equipment such as the state-of-the-art oceanographic research vessel Donghaero (150-ton class), ultrasonic current gauge (ADCP), and continuous temperature and salinity detector (CTD). The observed data was analyzed and used as basic data to support the hosting of the Windsurfing World Championship to be held at Gyeongpo Beach in Gangneung in September next year and to identify various marine phenomena in the region. It is expected that it will be utilized.
As a result of this investigation, it was found that the direction of the ocean current in the Gangneung frontal sea area tends to flow mostly northward, regardless of time. This is consistent with the general flow of the east coast of Korea in the summer, but the strength of the current was found to vary by about 0.5 knots depending on the location.
An official from the Korea Hydrographic and Oceanographic Agency added, "However, since this survey was conducted for the first time in the Gangneung region, the observation data accumulated so far is insufficient, so continuous surveys are needed to understand marine phenomena more accurately."
He also said, “We plan to continue to do our best to provide a variety of marine information services that satisfy consumers by conducting marine surveys that reflect the opinions and regional characteristics of marine information consumers.”

ko-news-notices-215-8372c75064.title: Incheon coastal islands marine environment survey, conservation, and management plan establishment service
ko-news-notices-215-8372c75064.text:
Incheon coastal islands marine environment survey, conservation, and management plan establishment service
2022-03-02
Commencement of marine environment survey, conservation, and management plan establishment service for Incheon coastal islands
Reporter Ham Sang-hwan
Incheon City commissioned Inha University's West Sea Coastal Environment Research Center (hereinafter referred to as the Research Center) to establish a conservation and management plan for the marine environment of the islands off the coast of Incheon and the surrounding coast and establish conservation and sustainable use measures.
Accordingly, the research center will establish the scope of the land and surrounding intertidal zone of 155 inhabited and uninhabited islands off the coast of Incheon and begin investigation and research over a period of 24 months until September 25, 2007 in order to survey the humanities, society, and natural ecology of the islands off the coast of Incheon and the surrounding coast, and build a research database.
The main research contents to be carried out during the period are ▶ Island humanities and social environment survey ▶ Island land and marine topography, geology, landscape fauna and flora, etc. ▶ Survey of natural environment such as island land and marine topography, geology, landscapes, animals and flora ▶ Survey of terrestrial natural disturbance, development, use status and pollution situation ▶ Survey of island fisheries status and surrounding awareness ▶ DB of survey data and establishment of GIS and web service ▶ Evaluation of island ecological carrying capacity ▶ Evaluation of island ecological capacity ▶ Survey of island fisheries status and pollution status Establishment of marine conservation and use standards ▶ Establishment of sustainable island marine environment conservation and management plan, etc.
The survey research method divides 155 books into 20 key books and 20 general survey books. The key survey books are intensively investigated, and the books are divided into 9 regions, including Yeongheung, Yeongjong, Deokjeok, Jawol, Jangbong, Baengnyeong, Yeonpyeong, Ganghwa, and Jumun, and compare and analyze their characteristics.
In addition, uninhabited islands are divided into special islands and general islands designated by the Ministry of Environment, and general islands are comprehensively divided into conservation islands, semi-preservation islands, and use islands. For field surveys, location information using GPS is recorded and used to build GIS.
To understand the status of the islands, we use field survey data and recent data from government agencies and important research institutes such as the Ministry of Environment, Ministry of Oceans and Fisheries, and Incheon City.
Establish a management and preservation plan for books by classifying them into used books.
Meanwhile, 20 islands, including Yeongjongdo, Yongyudo, Daemuido, Ganghwado, Gyodongdo, Seokmodo, Boreumdo, Jumundo, Yeongheungdo, Seonjaedo, Jawoldo, Seungbodo, Daeijakdo, Jangbongdo, Sindo, Shido, Deokjeokdo, Baengnyeongdo, Daecheongdo, and Daeyeonpyeongdo, will be intensively investigated.
Incheon = Reporter Ham Sang-hwan

ko-news-notices-214-8372c75064.title: [Oceanographic survey] Haeundae white sand beach is changing
ko-news-notices-214-8372c75064.text:
[Oceanographic survey] Haeundae white sand beach is changing
2022-03-02
Typhoon “Nabi” changed the white sand beach of Haeundae.
Korea Hydrographic and Oceanographic Agency's South Sea Oceanographic Survey Office (Director Jae-seop Lee) and the Pukyong National University Remote Sensing Center (Professor Cheol-woong Choi) jointly conducted a topographical survey of Haeundae Beach, the largest in Korea, and confirmed that typhoons are affecting the topographical changes of the white sand beach.
This survey used a precision satellite positioning system (GPS) to closely examine the topography of the white sand beach before (August 20 - August 21) and after (September 19 - September 20) the passage of Typhoon “Nabi,” and as a result of analyzing this data by combining it with aerial photos and satellite images, the area of the white sand beach increased (2,509.91 m2) due to sand deposition on Dongbaek Island, west of Haeundae Beach. The eastern Mipo side was found to have been eroded (4,316.45㎡) by exposing gravel and rocks due to sand loss.
In addition, it was revealed that the total white sand beach area of ​​Haeundae Beach decreased by 3,096 m2 from 56,537 m2 before the typhoon to 53,441 m2 after the typhoon, and the slope of the white sand beach was gently modified after the typhoon passed.
An official from the Korea Hydrographic and Oceanographic Agency said, “The results of this survey will be reflected in the ‘beach information map’ to promote the safety and convenience of users, as well as provide information necessary for local government beach management, and we plan to continuously monitor changes in the beach topography in the future.”

ko-news-notices-213-8372c75064.title: Jeju coastal marine environment information ‥ Promoting the establishment of a real-time measurement system
ko-news-notices-213-8372c75064.text:
Jeju coastal marine environment information ‥ Promoting the establishment of a real-time measurement system
2022-03-02
The establishment of a system to measure marine environmental information off the coast of Jeju in real time by applying the Ubiquitous Sensor Network (USN) is being promoted.
The Korea National Computerization Agency recently began the process of selecting field test research projects to discover USN application service models, and announced on the 23rd that a total of 8 projects, including ‘Establishment of a USN-based Jeju coastal marine environmental information collection system’, have been received and are being reviewed.
USN, a network configured to wirelessly collect information detected by various sensors, is a basic infrastructure network to accelerate social ubiquitization through sensor technology. A total of four models will be selected.
The Korea National Computerization Agency is highly likely to adopt the USN pilot project project in the future if the demand and effectiveness of sensor application are high as a result of field experiments, so it is receiving great interest from domestic and foreign businesses related to RFID (electronic tags).
The proposal submitted by SysNeck Co., Ltd. includes a plan to continuously manage seawater temperature and dissolved oxygen amount by collecting marine ecological information in real time using a wireless network in the 2.45GHz band along the Jeju coast.
To this end, the u-sensor network system will be installed on the coast of Jeju using standard buoys, and closed-circuit television (CCTV) capable of real-time monitoring will be installed.
It is expected that by collecting marine environmental information 24 hours a day, changes in sea temperature and the occurrence of harmful red tides can be detected early and changes can be tracked in real time, minimizing damage to fisheries.
<Reporter Hyeon Bong-cheol>hbc@jejunews.com

ko-news-notices-212-8372c75064.title: Seminar held to commemorate the 56th anniversary of the founding of the Korea Hydrographic and Oceanographic Agency
ko-news-notices-212-8372c75064.text:
Seminar held to commemorate the 56th anniversary of the founding of the Korea Hydrographic and Oceanographic Agency
2022-03-02
Ocean Research Institute holds a seminar to overcome the era of change
Korea Hydrographic and Oceanographic Agency (President Jong-rok Park) will celebrate its 56th anniversary on November 1 by inviting figures and seniors from various fields in the maritime field to a commemorative ceremony and seminar on future development directions at the Incheon Paradise Hotel.
About 100 people, including the Vice Minister of the Ministry of Oceans and Fisheries, oceanographers, associations, industry officials, and marine research staff, are expected to attend this seminar. There will be presentations by experts in each field and discussions among attendees about the role and importance of ocean research institutes appropriate for the new ocean era, and the direction of organizational development.
On this day, Dr. Seok-Woo Lee of Marine Science and Technology Co., Ltd., Professor Lim-Sang Oh of Seoul National University, Professor Joong-Ki Choi of the Korean Society of Oceanography, and Dr. Hoe-Soo Jeong of the Korea Ocean Research & Development Institute will give presentations on the topics that marine researchers must tackle in the future: strengthening organizational expertise, strengthening marine surveillance activities in response to climate change, cooperation with related organizations for tsunami reduction, and the importance of precise marine survey data that can scientifically prove changes in the coastal environment.
An official from the Korea Ocean Research Institute said, “This seminar will provide an opportunity for the Korea Ocean Research Institute to respond to the recently expanding demand for ocean research and establish a direction for transformation suitable for the new maritime era.”

ko-news-notices-211-8372c75064.title: ‘Deep ocean water well-being’ right before your eyes
ko-news-notices-211-8372c75064.text:
‘Deep ocean water well-being’ right before your eyes
2022-03-02
It is expected that various products using deep ocean water will be introduced in earnest as early as next year.
The Ministry of Oceans and Fisheries announced on the 18th that the results of deep water research and development will be visible and that it will be commercialized across various industries, including drinking water and cosmetics, starting next year.
Eight domestic companies, including Dongwon F&B (green tea beverage), Kooksoondang (distilled soju), and Aekyung Industrial (cosmetics), are participating in the deep water commercialization project, and the Ministry of Oceans and Fisheries explained that these companies will be able to produce prototypes by December of this year.
Deep water collected from a depth of less than 200m is a clean water resource rich in nutrients and almost free of organic matter or pathogens. Countries such as Japan and the United States have been producing products using deep water in earnest since 1990. In particular, in Japan, the market size reaches 2 trillion won per year.
In Korea, seaweed farming using deep water was conducted on a pilot basis last year, and the growth rate was found to be up to twice as fast as that of general surface water. It is expected to be used in a variety of fields not only in manufacturing but also in agriculture and fisheries.
However, when developing deep water into drinking water, the price is about 1.5 times that of commercially available drinking spring water, so reducing the unit cost of production is a challenge.
The Ministry of Oceans and Fisheries plans to build a deep ocean water research center in Ohori, Jukwang-myeon, Goseong-gun, Gangwon-do by November for full-scale research and development of deep water. Here, deep water is brought to land through a water intake pipe from a depth of 300 to 500 m, and after desalinization work, it is supplied to domestic research institutes and companies.
Kim Hyun-joo, director of the Korea Ocean Research & Development Institute's Deep Water Research Center, said, "If deep water research begins in earnest, an era in which Korea will also utilize deep water as a new industrial energy source will begin in earnest."
〈Reporter Choi Byung-tae cbt@kyunghyang.com〉

ko-news-notices-210-8372c75064.title: Will the cause of coastal sand erosion be revealed?
ko-news-notices-210-8372c75064.text:
Will the cause of coastal sand erosion be revealed?
2022-03-02
Jeju City establishes monitoring system at Iho Beach
Will the cause of sand erosion occurring at most beaches in the province be scientifically revealed?
Jeju City is attracting attention by establishing a sand erosion monitoring system at Iho Beach to determine the cause of sand erosion at the beach.
In particular, sand erosion is occurring at most beaches in the province, so it is expected that a solution to sand erosion can be derived based on the results of this survey.
Jeju City announced on the 18th that it had installed equipment for observing the coastline and waves in a building near Iho Beach.
It includes three video and Internet devices, and the observation data is sent in real time to the service provider, GeoSR Co., Ltd.
Jeju City estimates that the operation period of the monitoring system will take at least 3 to 5 years to analyze the causes of sand erosion, prepare countermeasures, and conduct post-verification.
Based on the survey results, Jeju City decided to maximize the function of Iho Beach by preparing efficient restoration measures for Iho Beach.
Currently, bedrock and pebbles are exposed throughout the white sandy beach of Iho Beach, which is 250m long and 120m wide, as the sand has eroded over the years.
In addition, sand erosion is occurring at most beaches in the province, including Hamo and Jungmun Beach, so the survey results are expected to be of great help in solving the problems there.
In relation to this, an official from Jeju City said, "This survey is being conducted as part of the monitoring system establishment project that the Ministry of Oceans and Fisheries is conducting in 22 locations across the country to solve the problem of coastal erosion."
Reporter Park Sang-seop (2005-10-19)

ko-news-notices-209-8372c75064.title: Real-time maps of seawater circulation around Yeosu become available online
ko-news-notices-209-8372c75064.text:
Real-time maps of seawater circulation around Yeosu become available online
2022-03-02
Real-time seawater current observations provided online for the first time
The Korea Hydrographic and Oceanographic Agency (Director General Jong-rok Park) announced that seawater circulation around Yeosu would be available online at http://www.nori.go.kr from October 19.
The many islands around Yeosu Bay create complex geography. Currents vary greatly over time and space with typhoons and river inflow. Increasing cargo volumes at coastal industrial complexes such as Gwangyang Steel Works also produce frequent vessel traffic making real-time current information essential.
Four coastal HF radars observe circulation over the broad area from Yeosu Bay to the waters around Namhae Island.
HF radar transmits high-frequency radio waves from land stations and observes surface currents using the phase difference in the reflected signal. It enables continuous observation even during adverse weather such as typhoons.
An agency representative expected the service to improve port traffic control and contribute to the safety of navigating and fishing vessels oil spill response and measures to address the spread of red tides.

ko-news-notices-208-8372c75064.title: Commencement of preparation of national port hinterland complex roadmap
ko-news-notices-208-8372c75064.text:
Commencement of preparation of national port hinterland complex roadmap
2022-03-02
Commencement of preparation of national port hinterland complex roadmap
Ministry of Oceans and Fisheries begins research service this month... Announcement in the second half of next year
Creation date: 2005.10.18
Research services to prepare a road map for the port hinterland complex, which contains the development scale and priorities of the hinterland complexes for each of the 28 trade ports nationwide, will begin in earnest starting this month.
As a result of the study, the comprehensive plan for the port hinterland complex is scheduled to be announced in the second half of next year.
To this end, the Ministry of Oceans and Fisheries announced the selection of a service provider for the ‘Establishment of a comprehensive plan for the development of a port hinterland complex for national trade ports’ last August and announced that it selected Geonil Engineering as the service manager and Geonhwa Engineering and Hangdo Engineering as partners.
The Ministry of Oceans and Fisheries also formed a working group in which the Northeast Asia Logistics Planning Group of the Ministry of Oceans and Fisheries, the Korea Research Institute for Human Settlements, and the Korea Trade-Investment Promotion Agency (KOTRA) participated.
In this port hinterland complex plan, a comprehensive plan is prepared to gradually develop the optimal hinterland complex to support port functions on idle land in 28 trade ports across the country, including Busan Port, Pyeongtaek, and Dangjin Port.
The Ministry of Oceans and Fisheries explained that, through this service, “it will serve as a blueprint for the development of the port hinterland complex encompassing the development demands of each port,” and that “by dividing it into 2011, 2016, and 2020, the scale of development of the hinterland complex required will be revealed considering the volume of traffic and cargo characteristics for each port.”
It was also decided to review ways to diversify the current hinterland development method, which focuses on the container terminal support complex, into containers, general cargo, and marine waterfront space in accordance with the characteristics of each region and port.
In addition, it was decided to actively reflect the opinions of global shippers and domestic logistics experts from the beginning of plan establishment in order to change the development method of the port hinterland logistics complex from a uniform site development-centered development method to a ‘Customerized’ port hinterland logistics complex development method that takes into account the demand (occupation time, required area, etc.) of port users such as global shippers and logistics companies.
The port hinterland complex is a space where various value-added activities such as storage, classification, assembly, distribution, and water-friendly space of cargo are carried out in the hinterland of the port. Major ports around the world, such as Rotterdam and Singapore, are operated based on the ‘value ton’ concept that focuses not only on cargo processing at the port but also on enhancing the added value of the port.
The Port of Rotterdam in the Netherlands, the gateway to Europe, ranked 7th in the world with 8.3 million TEU in terms of cargo traffic in 2003, but created an added value of $24.5 billion per year.
■Inquiries: Port Bureau Port Policy Division Kang Beom-gu Manager Yoon Du-han 02-3674-6712 / F 3674-6716

ko-news-notices-207-8372c75064.title: 1 trillion won invested in developing 9 new ports
ko-news-notices-207-8372c75064.text:
1 trillion won invested in developing 9 new ports
2022-03-02
Ministry of Oceans and Fisheries increases next year's facility budget by 5.2%
The Ministry of Oceans and Fisheries has decided to invest a total of 1.7828 trillion won next year for new port development and major port facility projects.
The Ministry of Oceans and Fisheries announced on the 28th that it has set aside 1.782868 trillion won as next year's port sector budget, a 1.09% increase from this year's 1.7635 trillion won.
In particular, it was decided to invest KRW 1.0352 trillion in the development of 9 new ports, including Busan New Port, which is a 5.2% increase from this year (KRW 983.8 billion).
In relation to this, the Ministry of Oceans and Fisheries stated that there is a need to expand facility projects and urgently improve infrastructure related to the port hinterland complex in order to become the logistics center of Northeast Asia.
Accordingly, the Ministry of Oceans and Fisheries set a facility budget of 468.3 billion won for Busan New Port, an increase of 4.4% from this year, and decided to invest 274 billion won in Gwangyang Port.
In addition, facility project costs of KRW 71.7 billion are planned to be allocated to Pyeongtaek Port, KRW 63.9 billion to Incheon North Port, KRW 90.7 billion to Ulsan New Port, and KRW 40.4 billion to Yeongilman New Port, and to Incheon South Outer Port.
An official from the Ministry of Oceans and Fisheries explained, “In order to quickly realize the logistics center of Northeast Asia, we focused on improving competition in attracting foreign exchange cargo, including expanding port infrastructure and improving the efficiency of port operations.”
In particular, he emphasized that he plans to actively work on early supply of the hinterland complex to create a foundation for attracting multinational logistics companies in the hinterland complex.
Accordingly, the Ministry of Oceans and Fisheries plans to spend 3.3877 trillion won on the Busan New Port construction project until this year to achieve 37% of the total process, and next year, it plans to continue to promote the construction of 13 berths for the North private sector project and 5 berths for the finance project, including the South pier.
Gwangyang Port also plans to invest 2.7293 trillion won by the end of the year to improve the overall process by 41% and focus on the 7-berth construction project of the 3-1 and 2 phase projects next year.
In addition, along with the construction of 100,000 pyeong of the eastern hinterland logistics complex, it was decided to supply the remaining logistics complex and functional facility land of 490,000 pyeong by 2008.
We plan to carry out basic survey design next year to supply 530,000 pyeong of western hinterland by 2011.
In addition, the Ministry of Oceans and Fisheries set a budget of 233.7 billion won, down 11.2% from this year, for major facility projects at six ports, including Busan Port and Incheon Port.
By port, 73.8 billion won is invested in Busan Port, 60.4 billion won in Gunsan Port, 34 billion won in Mokpo Port, 31.9 billion won in Jeju Port, 24 billion won in Incheon Port, and 9.4 billion won in Ulsan Port. The Ministry of Oceans and Fisheries also invested 123 billion won, an 8.7% increase from this year, in the construction projects of 28 trade ports, and 30% more than this year in the construction projects of 23 coastal ports. A reduced amount of 36.4 billion won was set.
In addition, the Ministry of Oceans and Fisheries decided to invest 140.7 billion won in port facility maintenance and 211.6 billion won in support for the container terminal complex.

ko-news-notices-206-8372c75064.title: Severe water pollution in the lower Han River
ko-news-notices-206-8372c75064.text:
Severe water pollution in the lower Han River
2022-03-02
It is not a new phenomenon that pollution along the Incheon coast is at a serious level. The water quality has long since deteriorated to level 3 water, which is difficult for fish and shellfish to live in, and fish contaminated with heavy metals have been caught, so it can no longer be left unattended. The root cause of coastal pollution is the influx of large amounts of rotten water from the Han River Estuary.
According to government audit data, 80% of all pollutants along the Incheon coast flow from the Han River. The water quality of the Han River Estuary, which flows into the salt sewer between Ganghwa Island and Gimpo, is more seriously polluted due to the influx of large amounts of various wastes. About one-third of the pollutants that float into the Han River flow into the salt sewage channel. About 20% of the fish caught here are deformed, with bent backs and rashes, and you can guess the reality by looking at them.
Nevertheless, the problem is that a comprehensive management system for the Han River Estuary is not in place, making it almost a blind spot. Centering on Yudo, an island in the lower Han River located on the border between Gimpo and Ganghwa, the river law applies to the right side and is under the jurisdiction of the Ministry of Environment, while the left side is under the jurisdiction of the Ministry of Oceans and Fisheries. The administrative district is divided into Incheon and Gyeonggi-do. As such, it is natural that pollution control in the Han River Estuary is not carried out efficiently due to lack of unification in the management system. Seoul, Gyeonggi, and Incheon are sharing treatment costs to improve marine pollution, but it is insufficient to deal with coastal pollution.
The importance of the ocean, which has infinite resources, cannot be overemphasized.
