The estuary where the river and the sea meet is rich in nutrients, and various creatures live and spawn, and migratory birds arrive, making the natural scenery beautiful. As these precious resources are not properly managed and neglected, the ecosystem is increasingly being destroyed. It goes without saying that if left unattended, the ecosystem will fall into a state of no recovery even though it is turning into a dead sea that is polluted to the point where it is difficult for fish and shellfish to survive.
If indifference to sea pollution and neglect of management ultimately devastate coastal fishing grounds and dry up fish, it would be a huge loss not only to the livelihoods of fishermen but also to the national economy. We must be deeply aware of the seriousness of coastal pollution and make efforts to preserve the marine environment. It is necessary to form a consultative body between central ministries and local governments and quickly prepare an organization and comprehensive measures to systematically manage the Han River Estuary.

ko-news-notices-205-8372c75064.title: Emergence of environmental issues in Gunjang Industrial Complex
ko-news-notices-205-8372c75064.text:
Emergence of environmental issues in Gunjang Industrial Complex
2022-03-02
Environmental issues are also emerging in the Gunjang Industrial Complex development project, increasing the possibility that they will become an obstacle to the smooth progress of the project.
This is because the Tidal Flat Ecosystem of the Geumgang Estuary has been seriously destroyed due to the Gunsan-Janghang National Industrial Complex development project, and the National Assembly's Foreign Exchange and Labor Committee pointed out that there should be a full reexamination.
Uri Party lawmaker Kim Young-joo (proportional representative), who is a member of the National Assembly's Environment and Labor Committee, said in a state audit of the Geumgang River Basin Environmental Office on the 6th that the Janghang District development project in the Gunjang National Industrial Complex is likely to destroy the tidal flat ecosystem and estuary ecosystem, and called for a full review of the project.
Rep. Kim pointed out that five class 1 species, including the yellow-billed egret, spoon-billed sandpiper, and spoonbill, and 14 class 2 species, including the black-fronted plover, designated as endangered wild animals by the Ministry of Environment, inhabit this area, and that more than 30,000 birds inhabit nearby Daejuk Island and other areas, and that destruction of the ecosystem is inevitable if the development of the Gunjang Industrial Complex continues.
Rep. Kim also claimed that this area has a very high conservation value worldwide, and that the Ministry of Oceans and Fisheries and the Environmental Policy Research Institute also presented opinions of ‘careful review’, predicting that the Gunjang Industrial Complex development plan would lead to environmental destruction.
In response to this, Hee-man Son, head of the Geumgang River Basin Environmental Office, said, "We have already received a supplementary evaluation through one request for supplementation of the environmental impact assessment, but it is still insufficient, so we have requested re-supplementation." He added, "We will form an environmental impact assessment council related to development and decide our position."/Seoul = Reporter Seungryeol Yoo․yous@

ko-news-notices-204-8372c75064.title: Commencement of detailed investigation into risk factors at Busan New Port anchorage
ko-news-notices-204-8372c75064.text:
Commencement of detailed investigation into risk factors at Busan New Port anchorage
2022-03-02
Korea Hydrographic and Oceanographic Agency's South Sea Ocean Research Office (Director Jae-seop Lee) announced on the 6th that it has begun a detailed seabed survey on the scheduled anchorage site on the eastern side of Gadeokdo Island to designate an anchorage site for Busan New Port.
In this survey, the marine research vessel “Namhaero” equipped with the latest equipment such as multibeam, global positioning system (GPS), and sound speed measuring instrument will be deployed to measure water depth and investigate the presence of navigational hazards and underwater obstacles on the seabed.
The results of this survey will produce seafloor topography and marine spatial information (3D seafloor topography, depth maps, etc.), and provide information such as changes in water depth and underwater obstacles necessary for designation of anchorages at Busan New Port, thereby supporting the designation and operation of anchorages in line with the opening of the new port scheduled for January 2006.
An official from the Korea Hydrographic and Oceanographic Agency said, “We expect to continue to produce the latest marine information such as water depth, seabed topography, currents, and tides for the new port and its vicinity, contributing to the development of the new port as a central hub port in Northeast Asia by providing information for safe navigation to users of the new port and vessels arriving and departing.”

ko-news-notices-203-8372c75064.title: Held a seminar on marine environment
ko-news-notices-203-8372c75064.text:
Held a seminar on marine environment
2022-03-02
The National Institute of Fisheries Science will hold a seminar in the small conference room of the Fisheries and Life Science Headquarters on October 11, 2005, with relevant researchers and academics in attendance.
The contents of this seminar include presentations on topics such as “Study on the Microscopic Biological Community Structure in the Southern and East China Seas in Summer” by Dr. Seung-min Lee of the West Sea Fisheries Research Institute and “Biological Assay Experiments and Utilization of Biological Activities of Biological Activities” by Dr. Seong-jin Yoon of the Galeun Research Institute. After this, attendees will gather in one place and have a comprehensive discussion on the topics.
Meanwhile, the harmful organisms team plans to reflect opinions from seminars and general discussions in the test research project.

ko-news-notices-202-8372c75064.title: Publication of ‘Tide Table’, a tide indicator along the Korean coast
ko-news-notices-202-8372c75064.text:
Publication of ‘Tide Table’, a tide indicator along the Korean coast
2022-03-02
Publication of ‘Tide Table’, a tide indicator along the Korean coast
Reporter Jo Soo-kyung camus0211@nate.com
Korea Hydrographic and Oceanographic Agency (President Jong-rok Park) announced that it had published the ‘Korean Coastal Tide Table’, which contains the tides of major ports along the Korean coast in 2006.
The tide table published this time forecasts the daily high and low tide times and sea level height for 47 major ports along the Korean coast, and includes tide forecasts for 14 narrow waterways. In particular, hourly forecast values ​​are included for Incheon Port, Gunsan Port, and Mokpo Port on the west coast and Busan Port on the south coast, which have large latitudes and many vessel operations.
In addition, the time difference and sea level height ratio compared to the reference port, which can roughly predict the tides of about 200 places along the coast of Korea other than the 47 reference ports, were included to enable a clear understanding of the tides of the entire coast, and the latest results on the basic level score table, which is the height standard for coastal development and port development, are also included.
An official from the Korea Hydrographic and Oceanographic Agency said, “This tide table is expected to be greatly utilized as useful data for navigators, port construction officials, the marine industry, and marine leisure activities.”
In the future, the Korea Hydrographic and Oceanographic Agency plans to quickly collect the latest domestic and international information related to navigation and publish and distribute various hydrographic publications. The Korean coastal tide table can be purchased through the national hydrographic book sales network (02-701-9981).

ko-news-notices-201-8372c75064.title: Commencement of ocean current survey in the East and South Seas
ko-news-notices-201-8372c75064.text:
Commencement of ocean current survey in the East and South Seas
2022-03-02
Korea Hydrographic and Oceanographic Agency (Director Jong-Rok Park) announced that it will conduct observations of ocean currents and physical characteristics of seawater in the sea area throughout the East and South Seas from October 1 to 31.
This survey is scheduled to simultaneously investigate ocean currents by water layer using an ultrasonic current monitor (ADCP), surface ocean currents using a satellite drifter (Argos Drifter), and seawater characteristics such as water temperature, salinity, dissolved oxygen, and pH. Badaro No. 2, a dedicated ocean observation vessel, will be mobilized.
The ocean current survey will be used to produce the Korean Standard Ocean Currents Map by identifying ocean currents and changes in sea conditions in our country's waters, which is expected to greatly contribute to ensuring the safety of ships and the development of oceanography.
The Korea Hydrographic and Oceanographic Agency will continue to conduct ocean current observations on a regular basis to understand the spatial and temporal characteristics of ocean currents and changes in the marine environment in the South Sea and the East Sea and post the results online (http://current.nori.go.kr We plan to provide services to consumers through a system that provides information on the physical characteristics of seawater) and navigation notifications.

ko-news-notices-200-8372c75064.title: Study finds thermal-discharge impact extends 20.2 km south of Yeonggwang Nuclear Power Plant
ko-news-notices-200-8372c75064.text:
Study finds thermal-discharge impact extends 20.2 km south of Yeonggwang Nuclear Power Plant
2022-03-02
(Yeonggwang = Yonhap News) Reporter Nam Hyun-ho = The final research results showed that the extent of damage caused by thermal discharge from Yeonggwang Nuclear Power Plant was 20.2km south from the power plant drain.
Yeonggwang Nuclear Power Plant announced on the 26th, "We have recently received the final report of the wide-area marine survey following the construction and operation of Yeonggwang Nuclear Power Plant Units 5 and 6, which was conducted by the Korea Ocean Research and Development Institute over a period of four years and four months from January 2001 to the end of last month."
According to the final research service report, the maximum extent of damage from thermal discharge to fishing grounds around the nuclear power plant was confirmed to be 20.2km south from the power plant drain.
This figure is based on the median value of 19.6-20.8km south, measured in August of last year, when the sea temperature was seasonally high and the inflow of thermal discharge into the fishing grounds was highest.
In addition, the maximum instantaneous extent of the 1°C temperature increase caused by thermal discharge was found to be 17.7-21.4 km south of the power plant drain measured in March 2002.
In addition, the average 1℃ diffusion distance (at low tide) before and after the construction of the discharge embankment, which was created as a measure to reduce thermal discharge, was found to be 12.3km and 11.8km to the south, respectively.
However, it is pointed out that this reduction has limitations in showing the average situation of the effect of the discharge embankment due to the lack of survey data prior to the construction of the discharge embankment.
This study was conducted to determine whether the role of the thermal discharge reduction facility after the operation of the six units of the Yeonggwang Nuclear Power Plant is suitable for the design value, to investigate the impact of thermal discharge on the ecosystem, to calculate the corresponding fishing damage rate when the impact is confirmed, and to provide basic data for calculating the fishing loss amount.
An official from the Korea Ocean Research and Development Institute, which performed the service, said, "In calculating the damage rate associated with thermal discharge, a comprehensive damage rate must be calculated by considering all factors in the marine environment, but there are practical difficulties in applying this. We did our best to resolve distrust between fishermen and the nuclear power plant through the fairness and objectivity of the research."
Yeonggwang Nuclear Power Plant, which received a report with such content, plans to soon conduct an appraisal of the fishing grounds within the damaged area to compensate for the damage to fishermen and determine the amount of compensation.
An official at Yeonggwang Nuclear Power Plant said, "Based on the interim report in May 2002, we have completed the first round of compensation of approximately 22 billion won to 2,500 households near the nuclear power plant. We plan to provide additional compensation as the final results are released."

ko-news-notices-199-8372c75064.title: Prepare measures to prevent coastal erosion
ko-news-notices-199-8372c75064.text:
Prepare measures to prevent coastal erosion
2022-03-02
Yangyang-gun, fact-finding service
Yangyang-gun is conducting a fact-finding service and preparing countermeasures to prevent coastal erosion, which is becoming increasingly severe.
Continuing from last year, Yangyang-gun plans to spend 30 million won this year to request services from the Kwandong University Maritime and Port Technology Research Center to analyze the extent and causes of coastal erosion on the coast of the Yangyang region and prepare countermeasures.
Accordingly, Kwandong University's Maritime and Port Technology Research Center will survey 38.5 km of the coastline from Mulchi-ri, Ganghyeon-myeon to Namae-ri, Hyeonnam-myeon, survey 20 km of the coastline, measure erosion and sedimentation, and conduct marine analysis, a numerical model experiment, by the end of this year.
Yangyang/Namjincheon jcnam@kado.net

ko-news-notices-198-8372c75064.title: Cultured pearl production using thermal discharge from a nuclear power plant
ko-news-notices-198-8372c75064.text:
Cultured pearl production using thermal discharge from a nuclear power plant
2022-03-02
Busan Regional Office of Oceans and Fisheries conducts Korea's first pearl nucleus insertion trial using this approach
A pilot project to produce cultured pearls using warm water discharged from a nuclear power plant is moving forward.
The Busan Regional Office of Oceans and Fisheries announced on the 21st that it had carried out nucleus insertion in cultivated pearl oysters after Korea's first successful pearl oyster cultivation trial using thermal discharge from a nuclear power plant.
The procedure involved 5000 pearl oysters about 7 cm long that had undergone grow-out and overwintering trials in 2003 using thermal discharge in the Daebyeon waters of Gijang-eup and the Wolnae waters of Jangan-eup in Gijang-gun Busan.
The procedure was carried out at a farm in Tongyeong Gyeongsangnam-do in July after conditioning including induced spawning through temperature stimulation and water depth adjustment.
The oysters with inserted nuclei will return to Wolnae waters the following month for overwintering. Pearl formation takes about one year and harvest is expected around October of the following year.
The office plans to disseminate the cultivation technology to provide an additional income source for farmers who mainly cultivate sea mustard kelp and other seaweeds.
Busan — Reporter Gi-hyeon Kim

ko-news-notices-197-8372c75064.title: Korea Hydrographic and Oceanographic Agency begins survey of ocean currents in the East China Sea
ko-news-notices-197-8372c75064.text:
Korea Hydrographic and Oceanographic Agency begins survey of ocean currents in the East China Sea
2022-03-02
Korea Hydrographic and Oceanographic Agency (President Jong-Rok Park) announced that it will conduct an ocean current survey jointly with Pusan ​​National University in the East China Sea, the inflow channel, from September 8 to September 14 to reveal the water circulation phenomenon in the Yellow Sea.
Through this joint ocean current survey, the Korea Hydrographic and Oceanographic Agency will measure the characteristics of seawater and real-time seawater flow using satellite tracking floats, and will investigate the distribution of planktonic particles in the East China Sea for the first time using a continuous particle detector and an ultrasonic current meter.
The East China Sea is not only the path of typhoons approaching our country, but also a passageway for numerous ships passing through the Yellow Sea and an important sea area where the Ieodo Comprehensive Oceanographic Observation Station is located. In order to research and utilize the seawater circulation in the Yellow Sea, investigation and understanding of the seawater circulation in the East China Sea must be conducted first.
In particular, a three-dimensional investigation of seawater flow is very important in studying the impact of the world's largest Shansha Dam, built on the Yangtze River in China, on Korean waters.
An official from the Korea Hydrographic and Oceanographic Agency said, “The results of this survey will be provided through the Institute’s website (www.nori.go.kr) in the future, and are expected to be used as important data in identifying marine phenomena in the East China Sea following the construction of China’s Shansha Dam.”

ko-news-notices-196-8372c75064.title: [News] East Sea sea level rise rate is twice the global average
ko-news-notices-196-8372c75064.text:
[News] East Sea sea level rise rate is twice the global average
2022-03-02
It has been shown that the average sea level rise rate in the East Sea over the past 10 years has far exceeded the global average rise rate. According to the results of the analysis of observational data obtained from high-altitude satellites by Dr. Seok-gu Kang's team at the Korea Ocean Research and Development Institute (Director: Yeomki University), the average annual sea level rise rate in the East Sea over the past 9 years was found to be 5.4 ± 0.3 mm/year, and in particular, the average annual rise rate in the southern part of the East Sea was found to be 6.6 ± 0.4 mm/year. This figure is approximately twice the global average annual sea level rise rate (2.8 mm ± 0.4 mm per year) during the same period. In addition, the research team was the first to identify that the main cause of the rise in sea level in the East Sea is the “thermal expansion effect” caused by the rise in water temperature in the upper layer of the East Sea. At a time when there has been a major debate in recent related research fields as to whether the main cause of sea level rise in the world's oceans over the past several decades to 100 years is the effect of the decline of land glaciers or the effect of thermal expansion, the results of this study are of great significance as they identify the main cause of the rise in basin-type seas such as the East Sea.
These research results were obtained during the “Elemental Technology Research for Climate Change Monitoring and Prediction” (research leader: Dr. Jaehak Lee), which is being carried out as a basic research project at the Korea Ocean Research Institute, and was conducted jointly with the Canadian Ocean Research Institute research team.
This study comprehensively utilized Earth observation altitude satellite (TOPEX/Poseidon) data, East Sea water temperature and salinity data, and sea level observation data from Korean and Japanese tide stations. Through their research paper, Dr. Kang's team suggested that the sea level change due to the thermal expansion effect of the East Sea is a long-term period of 10 to 20 years and is closely related to the heat balance changes in the North Pacific. In addition, it was pointed out that the recent rapid change may be part of a long-term change, and the need for continuous sea level monitoring in the East Sea in the future and research on the possibility of changes in the rising mechanism related to ocean fluctuations in the long term was raised. This paper was published in the July issue of the Journal of Geophysical Research, a leading journal in the field of earth science published by the American Geophysical Union, and is scheduled to be presented as an invited paper at the 14th meeting of the North Pacific Ocean Science Organization (PICES) to be held in Vladivostok in September.
With more than 2 billion people worldwide concentrated within 100 km of the coast, changes in sea level are evaluated as a major measure of climate change. Therefore, understanding the causes and quantitative rate of long-term sea level rise is of major interest to not only scientists but also the general public. Dr. Waleed Abdalati of NASA points out, “If sea levels rise by 1 meter, approximately 100 million people will be affected.” In the 1990s, scientists predicted that future sea levels would rise by about 50 cm (5 mm/year) over the next 100 years of the 21st century. However, through this study, it was found that the East Sea has already exceeded this rate of rise in the past 10 years since the early 1990s, and the global sea level rise rate during the same period is approximately 60% of the predicted level.
A paper contributed to Science last year by glaciologist Dr. R. Thomas and others pointed out that the rate of sea level rise is accelerating due to the recent influx of continental glaciers into the sea in the Amundsen Sea on the west side of Antarctica, and that glaciers in the Amundsen Sea basin alone contain an amount of fresh water that can raise the global sea level by 1.3 m. Considering the enormous amount of ice in Greenland and Antarctica, depending on the degree of warming, sea level rise may increase or the annual rate of rise may accelerate compared to current estimates. NASA is active in research in related fields, including launching an observation satellite (ICEsat) in 2003 whose main mission is to observe the mass balance of continental ice in Antarctica and Greenland.
Due to climate change, along with long-term sea level changes, short-term sea level oscillations are expected to increase. The warmer ocean, along with many other factors, ultimately contributes to the strengthening of typhoon intensity through ocean-typhoon interaction, which is expected to increase the intensity of the tsunami during the typhoon period. In addition to long-term sea level fluctuations, the Korea Ocean Research and Development Institute plans to promote research on short-term sea level fluctuations as a full-fledged national research project, such as short-term changes in intensity due to ocean-typhoon interaction, precise tsunami prediction technology, and development of prediction technology for the effect of rising ocean temperatures due to global warming on typhoon intensity, etc.

ko-news-notices-195-8372c75064.title: Korea Hydrographic and Oceanographic Agency holds public hearing on revision of subordinate laws of the Waterway Services Act
ko-news-notices-195-8372c75064.text:
Korea Hydrographic and Oceanographic Agency holds public hearing on revision of subordinate laws of the Waterway Services Act
2022-03-02
Gathering a wide range of opinions on major issues such as the scope of exemption from general hydrographic surveys
The Korea Hydrographic and Oceanographic Agency (President Jong-rok Park) held a public hearing on the revision of subordinate laws of the Waterway Services Act at 3:00 p.m. on September 1, 2005 in the conference room of the Korea Hydrographic and Oceanographic Agency in relation to the revision of subordinate laws of the Waterways Services Act.
At the public hearing on this day, July 29, 2005. As the Waterway Services Act was revised and promulgated, a wide range of opinions were collected from government and local government officials and related industry organizations in attendance to revise subordinate laws, including the scope of marine construction exempted from general waterway survey obligations, subdivision of waterway survey projects, and changes in registration standards.
In particular, in the case of long-term marine construction over several years, it was decided to review the plan of conducting a waterway survey upon partial completion of the construction by determining the degree of completion and availability of the construction and conducting a general waterway survey after the final completion of the construction, and reflect it in the laws and regulations appropriately.
In addition, there was no disagreement about subdividing the registered waterway survey business, which is one of the concerns of related businesses, into more subdivisions than the current one, but it was suggested that there may be difficulties in securing technical manpower for the time being as the waterway survey volume expands.
Meanwhile, in order to ensure accurate hydrographic surveying at an international level, the Korea Hydrographic and Oceanographic Agency emphasized the need to revise the registration standards for hydrographic projects, which are limited to those with experience and academic background in the relevant technical field.
An official from the Korea Hydrographic and Oceanographic Agency said, “We plan to review the contents of the public hearing discussed on this day and actively accept the parts that are feasible in the revision (draft).”
The amendment (draft) to the subordinate laws of the Waterway Affairs Act, which was held at this public hearing, will go into effect at the end of January next year if necessary procedures such as legislative notice are taken around mid-September and passed by the Cabinet meeting in December.

ko-news-notices-194-8372c75064.title: Korea Hydrographic and Oceanographic Agency, seawater flow survey around Hallyeohaesang National Park
ko-news-notices-194-8372c75064.text:
Korea Hydrographic and Oceanographic Agency, seawater flow survey around Hallyeohaesang National Park
2022-03-02
Korea Hydrographic and Oceanographic Agency (President Jong-rok Park) announced that it will conduct a seawater flow survey in the waters around Hallyeohaesang National Park from this month to early October.
The Korea Hydrographic and Oceanographic Agency explained that for this investigation, 10 buoy systems including surface flow meters were deployed in the waters surrounding Hallyeo Marine National Park (from Geoje Island to Namhae Island) to observe seawater flow continuously for more than a month.
The area around Hallyeo Marine National Park is visited by many tourists as it has beautiful maritime scenery and is a passageway to Yeosu and Samcheonpo. It is a sea area where harmful red tide occurs, and the surrounding fish farms are regularly damaged, so accurate seawater flow information is essential for marine tourism, safe navigation, and prediction of the spread of red tide.
An official from the Korea Hydrographic and Oceanographic Agency said, “These observation results will contribute to revitalizing maritime economic activities and protecting the marine environment by enabling us to provide accurate tidal current forecast services for major traffic routes and passages around Hallyeo Marine National Park.” He also requested that vessels passing near the observation area make efforts to protect the observation buoys to ensure successful observations.

ko-news-notices-193-8372c75064.title: Environmental impact assessment fees will increase starting next year.
ko-news-notices-193-8372c75064.text:
Environmental impact assessment fees will increase starting next year.
2022-03-02
“The environmental impact assessment fee will increase starting next year.”
There won’t be a big increase, but we will respect industry opinion.
Starting next year, the fee standards for preparing environmental impact assessments are expected to be raised.
The Ministry of Environment announced that it has decided to push for an increase in the compensation standard considering the trend of increasing environmental friendliness of development projects, raising concerns about insolvency due to the low standards for compensating environmental impact assessments.
The Ministry of Environment plans to conduct an internal review of the 'Notice on the Standards for Calculating Costs for Preparing Environmental Impact Statements', which was revised in March 2001, by October and prepare improvement measures for ▷direct expenses, ▷expenses, ▷technology fees, and ▷calculation of additional costs.
In particular, the plan is to reorganize evaluation items such as topography, geology, water quality, and cultural assets, as well as manpower requirements and cost estimation standards according to content.
An official from the Ministry of Environment said, “The increase in labor costs has continued to be applied in conjunction with the price fluctuation rate, so it is not a large increase, but we will reflect the opinions of the industry in our own way.” He added, “We will adjust the compensation standards according to the cost, difficulty, and completeness of preparing the environmental impact assessment report.”
In the future, this notice will be applied to the Ministry of Economy and Finance (Price Stabilization Act) and the Ministry of Science and Technology (Engineering Technology Promotion Act), so a final draft plan will be drawn after consultation with each ministry.
An official from the Environmental Impact Assessment Association said, “Considering that environmental impact assessment items and difficulty are increasing according to new social trends, there is an urgent need to make the compensation standards realistic.”
Reporter Jeong Jang-hee h2hideo@(Korea Construction Newspaper)

ko-news-notices-192-8372c75064.title: New tide observation station established on Geoje Island
ko-news-notices-192-8372c75064.text:
New tide observation station established on Geoje Island
2022-03-02
For the first time, wave height observations were also conducted.
The Korea Hydrographic and Oceanographic Agency (Director Jong-Rok Park) announced that it will establish a new tide station in Dojangpo Port, Geoje Island to monitor sea level changes caused by global environmental changes such as warming and observe wave heights due to typhoon invasion.
Geoje Island is home to many famous tourist destinations such as Oedo Island, Haegeumgang Island, and Maemuldo Island. It has a complex submarine topography, with strong tidal currents and frequent passage of ships, so the need for tide level observation to provide accurate tidal information has emerged.
Geoje Island Tidal Observatory, which will begin construction in mid-August this year, will observe sea level fluctuations (tides), sea water characteristics (water temperature, salinity, density), and sea conditions (temperature, wind direction, wind speed, atmospheric pressure) and provide the results in real time through the Korea Hydrographic and Oceanographic Agency website (www.nori.go.kr).
An official from the Korea Hydrographic and Oceanographic Agency said, 'Geoje Island is greatly affected by typhoons every year. Unlike tide stations installed in other areas, a wave gauge was installed near the tide station to monitor the height of waves during typhoons and bad weather. It is expected to be used as important data for preventing marine disasters by predicting the risk of wave heights and providing it to disaster prevention agencies.'
